title: Gradients: which way is downhill
numbers_from: media/school/gradients/facts.json, computed by tools/school/fill_gradients.mjs (the surfaces, and the attention lesson's trained model); tools/school/fill_script.mjs fills every double-brace token below from it

open.what: The hill above the harbour at night, in fog. Pylon climbs into the fog with her lantern; the harbour lights vanish behind her. No words.

close.what: The fog thins. Pylon is at the bottom of a valley, not the lowest one; she plants a cone there, looks at the next hill, and puts out the lantern.

segments.heading: Gradients
lines: Gradients. Which way is downhill.
Tonight the hill is in fog. I can't see the bottom. All I can do is feel the ground under my flippers.

segments.heading: Feel the slope
lines: Put one flipper a little to the east and feel how much higher the ground is there. That's the slope going east.
Do the same going north. Two slopes, written as a list: that list is the gradient.
The gradient points the steepest way up. So to go down, step the opposite way. Feel, step, feel again. That's gradient descent. Augustin Cauchy wrote it down in 1847.

segments.heading: How big a step
lines: Here is a bowl, steep one way and gentle the other: the steep way curves {{bowl.conditionNumber}} times as sharply as the gentle way.
Bigger steps should get me down faster, so let's double mine.

Over the edge. On this bowl, any step longer than two divided by the steep way's curvature, {{bowl.curvatures.0}}, overshoots further each time. That edge is {{bowl.predictedBound}}, and running the bowl puts it exactly there.
Half that step gets down smoothly. Just under the edge, I zigzag and crawl. Just over it, I zigzag outwards. At twice it, the loss passes a trillion in just {{bowl.runs.3.steps}} steps.

predict.question: If I double my step, do I get down twice as fast?

segments.heading: A long, narrow valley
lines: Now a valley that is steep across and almost flat along. At the bottom, the steep way curves about {{rosenbrock.conditionNumberAtMinimum|int}} times as sharply as the flat way.

The steep way sets the largest safe step, so along the flat way I creep. It takes {{rosenbrock.firstStepBelow.1e-2|int}} steps to get the loss under a hundredth, and {{rosenbrock.firstStepBelow.1e-6|int}} to get it under a millionth.

segments.heading: Which valley
lines: One more hill, with two valleys and a ridge between them. I start just left of the ridge, then just right of it.
Different valleys. The right one is not even the lower one. Gradient descent finds a bottom near where it starts, not the lowest bottom there is.

predict.question: Do the two starts end in the same valley?

segments.heading: The model's own hill
lines: The language model from the attention lesson has {{gradientNorm.nParams|int}} numbers. Its loss is a hill with {{gradientNorm.nParams|int}} directions, and its gradient is a list of {{gradientNorm.nParams|int}} slopes.
Before training, the length of that list was {{gradientNorm.init.rows256.norm|f2}}. After training it is {{gradientNorm.trained.rows256.norm|f2}}: the ground under the trained model is much flatter.

To see any of it, we cut a slice through the trained point along two random directions, the way Li and colleagues did in 2018. The loss is {{landscape.trained.center|f2}} in the middle and climbs to {{landscape.trained.max|f2}} at one corner.

One warning. In a hill with {{gradientNorm.nParams|int}} directions, two random ones are almost at right angles to the steepest one. This slice shows that the model sits in a dip along these two directions. It cannot show the whole hill.

segments.heading: One number, by hand
lines: So let's follow one direction we choose. Freeze every number, and add one dial that turns the model's last matrix up or down. At one, it's the model as trained.

On sentences it never trained on, the bottom of this one-way slice is at {{oneNumber.sStar|f2}}, not at one, though the loss there is only a hair lower. Turning the dial down makes the model a little less sure of itself, and new text likes that.

Start the dial near zero, feel the slope with the model's own arithmetic, and step. With small steps, forty of them walk the dial up to {{oneNumber.descents.1.end|f2}}. A step too big for the steep ground near zero overshoots to well past one, and has to walk back.

segments.heading: What the fog hides
lines: This model's training never feels the whole hill at once. Each step feels the slope on {{batch}} short stretches of text, so every step is a little off.
And I haven't said how a model with {{gradientNorm.nParams|int}} numbers works out {{gradientNorm.nParams|int}} slopes at once without feeling each one separately. That's the bucket chain, next.

segments.heading: Goodnight
lines: The gradient is the list of slopes. Step the other way, not too far, and you go down. Where you end up depends on where you start.
Next along the hill: blame, passed backwards. Goodnight.
